classification.difficultyReason: Form an area function by subtracting two triangles, then differentiate and justify its greatest value.

content.prompt:
$ABCD$ is a square of unit length.

Points $E$ and $F$ are on the sides $AB$ and $AD$ respectively so that $AE=AF=x$.

spec.description: Unshaded square with A bottom left, B bottom right, C top right and D top left. E is on AB and F on AD; FE and EC partition the square. Both AE and AF carry x labels. Coordinates reproduce the illustrative placement without supplying a numerical value of x.
spec.mathematics: AB=BC=CD=DA=1; AE=AF=x. The required quadrilateral is CDFE.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied vertex names and two x labels are visible.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Express the area of the quadrilateral $CDFE$ as a function of $x$.

answer.worked:
Subtract triangles $CBE$ and $FEA$ from the square. Since $BE=1-x$,
$$\begin{align*}A(x)&=A_{ABCD}-A_{CBE}-A_{FEA}\\A(x)&=1^2-\frac{1(1-x)}{2}-\frac{x^2}{2}\\A(x)&=\frac12+\frac{x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{2}.\end{align*}$$
The side restrictions give $0\le x\le1$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the greatest area that the quadrilateral can have.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}A'(x)&=\frac12-x.\end{align*}$$
At a stationary point,
$$\begin{align*}0&=\frac12-x\\x&=\frac12.\end{align*}$$
Since $A''(x)=-1<0$ throughout the domain, this gives the greatest area.
$$\begin{align*}A\left(\frac12\right)&=\frac12+\frac14-\frac18\\A\left(\frac12\right)&=\frac58.\end{align*}$$
The greatest area is $\frac58$ square units.
